title: Code interpreter and sandboxes
summary: The model writes code and a sandbox runs it, so the agent can calculate, analyse files and draw charts. The code is untrusted, so isolation, per-user sessions and egress limits matter more than the model.
useIf: The task needs exact calculation, file or data analysis, or chart generation, and you can run model-written code in an isolated environment.
avoidIf: A plain API or MCP tool already does the job, or you would run the code in the same process or container as your secrets.

explain.md: A **code interpreter** gives the model a tool that executes code, usually Python, and returns output, files and errors. The model loops: write code, read the result, fix and retry. It turns arithmetic, data analysis and plotting from guesses into computed results. The code comes from a model that may have read attacker text, so treat it as **untrusted code**.

explain.title: One turn of a code-interpreter loop
explain.alt: The user asks, the app calls the model, the model returns code, the app runs it in a per-user sandbox session, and the output goes back to the model for the answer.
explain.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant A as App
  participant M as Model
  participant S as Sandbox session
  U->>A: Question and file
  A->>M: Prompt and tool
  M->>A: Python code
  A->>S: Run with session id
  S->>A: Output and files
  A->>M: Tool result
  M->>A: Answer

explain.md: **Azure Container Apps dynamic sessions** run code interpreter sessions isolated by a Hyper-V boundary, designed for untrusted code. The **session identifier** is a caller-defined string. It is treated as sensitive, and your app must ensure each user or tenant reaches only its own sessions. A session pool allows up to 600 concurrent sessions, an idle cooldown of 300 to 3600 seconds and outbound network `EgressDisabled` by default. Python sessions include NumPy, pandas and scikit-learn [[r32]] [[r33]]. Doc samples use the preview REST version `2025-10-02-preview`, so check API status before depending on it [[r32]].

The **Foundry Code Interpreter** tool runs Python in a sandbox for agents. It has charges beyond token fees. Two simultaneous conversations create two sessions, and each session is active for one hour by default with a 30-minute idle timeout [[tr1]]. Code Interpreter is among the tools supported under Foundry network isolation [[r27]].

explain.title: Egress is the exfiltration path
explain.md: If the sandbox can reach the internet, injected code can send your files out. Keep egress disabled, pass data in as files and put network calls behind separate, reviewed tools.

whereToUse: Analysing uploaded spreadsheets and CSV files and producing charts
Exact arithmetic and unit conversions that models get wrong when they guess
File format conversions and data cleaning inside an agent
Computer-use alternatives: code against a page (for example Playwright) in an isolated runtime
Education or notebook-style assistants where users run model-written code

use: The task is computable and a checked result beats a guess
You can isolate each user or tenant in its own session
Egress can stay off and data goes in as files
avoid: Running model-written code in the app's own process or a container with secrets
Letting the client choose the session identifier
flips: Packages or data need the internet: pre-stage them or add a reviewed tool instead of opening egress
Many short, stateless calls: per-request sessions may be cheaper than long-lived ones
Platform charges per session dominate: pool or share sessions only within one user's trust boundary

pitfalls.symptom: One user's files appear in another user's session
pitfalls.cause: Session identifiers were guessable, shared or supplied by the client
pitfalls.fix: Derive the identifier server side from the authenticated user and conversation, treat it as sensitive and check ownership on every call.

pitfalls.cause: Each concurrent conversation creates its own session with its own charges
pitfalls.fix: Cap concurrency, tune idle cooldown and timeouts and meter sessions per tenant.

pitfalls.cause: Egress was enabled and injected code made outbound calls
pitfalls.fix: Keep egress disabled, stage files in and out through your app and log every execution.

scenarios.title: Employee data assistant
scenarios.situation: Employees upload spreadsheets and ask for analysis and charts. No internet access is needed. Each person's files are confidential to them.
unknowns: How many concurrent users at peak?
Do sessions need to persist across days?
scenarios.question: Where does the code run?

options.name: In the app's own container, to keep things simple
options.why: Model code would share a process with your secrets and network.
options.tradeoff: Only acceptable for a throwaway local prototype with no sensitive data.

options.name: Dynamic sessions with a per-user session id and egress disabled
options.why: Hyper-V isolation, per-user sessions and no outbound access fit untrusted code and confidential files.
options.tradeoff: You build pool sizing and session id ownership checks.

options.name: The Foundry Code Interpreter tool
options.why: Least build effort when the agent already runs on Foundry.
options.tradeoff: Per-session charges beyond tokens and less control over the runtime.

flips.if: The agent is already a Foundry agent and volume is small
flips.then: The Foundry tool may be the simpler best choice.
Use a self-managed sandbox and own its isolation.

scenarios.takeaway: Isolate by user and keep egress off for untrusted code.

scenarios.title: Analysis that needs an external dataset
scenarios.situation: The analysis needs a public dataset and extra Python packages that are not pre-installed. The team suggests enabling outbound access on the sandbox.
constraints: Packages and data come from the internet
unknowns: Can packages be pre-approved and staged?
Can the dataset be fetched by a tool instead?
scenarios.question: How do you provide the dependencies?

options.name: Enable open outbound access so code can fetch anything
options.why: Injected or mistaken code could also send sensitive files out.
options.tradeoff: Reasonable only for a sandbox that never sees sensitive data.

options.name: A separate reviewed tool fetches the dataset, and approved packages are staged in advance
options.why: Keeps the sandbox closed and the fetch auditable.
options.tradeoff: More engineering and a maintenance list of approved packages.

options.name: Keep egress disabled and pass the dataset in as a file the app retrieves
options.why: The app controls what enters the sandbox and nothing can leave on its own.
options.tradeoff: Dependencies must come with the session environment or be avoided.

flips.if: The sandbox only ever sees public data
flips.then: Limited egress is a lower risk.
Stage them through a reviewed build path, not at run time.

scenarios.takeaway: Bring data in through your app, not through open egress.

scenarios.title: SaaS product with client-supplied session ids
scenarios.situation: A SaaS app lets browser clients start analysis. A developer proposes the browser sends a session id so users can resume work.
constraints: Resuming sessions is a real user need
scenarios.question: How do you manage session identity?

options.name: Derive the id on the server from the authenticated user and conversation
options.why: The identifier is sensitive and the app must ensure users reach only their own sessions.

options.name: Accept any id the browser sends
options.why: A guessed or leaked id gives another user's session and files.
options.tradeoff: Fine only if ids are unguessable and checked against the owner on every call.

options.name: A fresh random session per request
options.tradeoff: Users lose resume, uploaded files and state each time.

flips.then: Store the mapping server side with an expiry.

scenarios.takeaway: Treat the session id like a credential and mint it on the server.

quiz.q: What is the default outbound network setting for Azure Container Apps session pools?
options: Allowed to a fixed list of Azure services
quiz.explain: Session pools default to `EgressDisabled`. Enabling egress is a deliberate choice that creates an exfiltration path.

quiz.q: A tenant reports seeing another tenant's files in a session. Which causes are plausible?
options: The client could choose the session identifier
quiz.explain: The identifier is a sensitive, caller-defined string and the app must scope it to a user. Pool size and disabled egress do not cause cross-tenant access.

quiz.q: Two simultaneous conversations call the Foundry Code Interpreter. What happens?
options: They share one session until the idle timeout expires
Two sessions are created, each billed beyond tokens
The second call waits in a queue until the first conversation ends
quiz.explain: Each simultaneous conversation creates its own Code Interpreter session. Sessions are active for one hour by default with a 30-minute idle timeout, and they carry charges beyond token fees.

flashcards.front: What isolates Azure Container Apps code interpreter sessions?
flashcards.back: A Hyper-V boundary, designed for untrusted code. Pools allow up to 600 concurrent sessions and default to egress disabled.

flashcards.front: Why is the dynamic session identifier sensitive?
flashcards.back: It is a caller-defined string that selects a session. Your app must ensure each user or tenant reaches only its own sessions.

flashcards.front: How long does a Foundry Code Interpreter session live by default?
flashcards.back: One hour active with a 30-minute idle timeout. Each simultaneous conversation creates its own session, billed beyond token fees.
